doc.title: Dick Hyman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 17, 2001 [interview 2 of 2]

title: The Drifters' White Christmas session and early rock
summary: Hyman recalls the Drifters session, four numbers in three hours, and early rock becoming classic.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: That’s so cool. Let’s talk about this. Because I went back and was reading your first interview actually and you mentioned some of the people you played with — Ruth Brown and the Coasters and the Drifters. And you made a comment about their version of “White Christmas.”
Oh yeah. That was a session we did “White Christmas” — was that the Drifters or the Coasters? © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-
I think it was the Drifters.

Yeah, I believe you’re right. The session included Jerry Wexler, who is a good friend of mine in Florida, he’s long retired, he points out that that session with the Drifters produced four hits. Not only “White Christmas” but “The Bells of St. Mary,” and two others which I can’t name. In those days you know, it was customary to do four numbers in a session. Now people take a month to do something and they track it and they change it and they mess around with it. Well the union contract specified four numbers in three hours. And many people did just that, even in pop records, or maybe you’d go into a half hour or an hour overtime, but four tunes was the norm. At any rate there was always something going on and I loved it.

You had said that. “we said to each other at that time in twenty years” — this was 1955 or so — “in twenty years people will say to each other ‘listen darling, they’re playing our song.’ You know that’s exactly what happened. All that funny music that we laughed at became classic rock.”

That’s true. That’s absolutely true. We’ve all lived to see that. When I see now the musicology that’s spent on early rock ‘n roll and the nostalgia and the way it’s permeated everything we do I just marvel at it. In those days we didn’t really respect it much. We just did it.
